Rows: A low pressure system developed over the lower Mississippi Valley on Tuesday February 13th, and then tracked northeast, reaching the mid Atlantic coast by Wednesday morning on February 14th, while intensifying. The storm continued to strengthen during the day on February 14th, before moving off the New England coast by Wednesday night.|The storm spread a swath of very heavy snowfall across eastern New York and western New England, which started during the late evening hours of Tuesday, and tapered off late Wednesday night.|Snowfall amounts ranged from 1 to 3 feet across the hardest hit areas of New York State, which included the Schoharie Valley, western Mohawk Valley, and southern Adirondacks.  Amounts as high as 40 to 42 inches occurred in portions of western Montgomery County and southern Herkimer County. Slightly lower amounts occurred across the lower mid Hudson Valley, where sleet mixed in with the snow.|This storm significantly impacted travel and commerce across the region from Wednesday through Thursday, as many schools and businesses were closed.  Many roadways became impassable by Wednesday afternoon.|In addition, in Wappingers Falls in western Dutchess County, a roof collapse occurred due to the weight of heavy sleet and snow accumulation on a structure.  Although 20 people were displaced, there were no reports of injuries.|Strong winds also created near blizzard conditions at times during Wednesday afternoon and evening.

Heavy snow fell overnight across the west central and central mountains and the adjacent highlands. Amounts along the Sandia crests east of Albuquerque reached 10 to 13 inches with 4 to 7 inches spread across metro Albuquerque. Satellite snow coverage and various reports showed 6 to 8 inches in the west towards Grants and Gallup, 5 to 10 inches in the central areas from Ruidoso north to Las Vegas and 2 to 5 inches east along Interstate 25 to Tucumcari.

Low pressure strengthened rapidly as it tracked from the mid Atlantic coast to Cape Cod. Snow began in northern Connecticut late in the evening on the 13th, before changing to a wintry mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain during the morning of the 14th. Although snowfall totals only averaged 2 to 5 inches, this was the season's first winter storm, and the combination of snow and ice resulted in hazardous travel conditions, especially for morning commuters.|Officially, the snowfall total at Bradley International Airport in Windsor Locks was 2.4 inches. Other snowfall totals, as reported by trained spotters and cooperative observers, included 5.2 inches in Tolland, 4.5 inches in North Granby and Vernon, 3.5 inches in Manchester, Staffordville, and Thompson, and 3 inches in Avon, Burlington, East Granby, and Somers.

Snowfall totals ranged from 2 inches in Farmington to 4.5 inches in North Granby, but light icing was reported throughout Hartford County from a combination of snow, sleet, and freezing rain which ended as a period of freezing drizzle.

Rows: Low pressure strengthened rapidly as it tracked from the mid Atlantic coast to Cape Cod. The season's first winter storm brought snow, sleet and freezing rain to interior sections of Massachusetts and heavy rain with strong northeast winds along the coast.|Snow began in western Massachusetts during the evening of the 13th and reached the coast by midnight. Milder air coming off the ocean caused the snow to change to sleet and freezing rain during the day on the 14th from the Mass Turnpike region into the Merrimack Valley, and to all rain in greater Boston and points south. Temperatures fell sharply late in the day and during the evening, causing a flash freeze and icy travel conditions. Precipitation changed back to snow before ending around midnight on the 15th.|The highest snowfall totals, on the order of 6 to 12 inches, were observed from the east slopes of the Berskhires to the Route 2 corridor and into the Merrimack Valley. Although snowfall totals only averaged 2 to 5 inches farther to the south, the combination of snow and ice resulted in hazardous travel conditions. Dozens of minor accidents were reported.|Official snowfall totals included 9.8 inches at Worcester Airport, 2.5 inches at Logan Airport in Boston, 2.1 inches at the National Weather Service office in Taunton, and 1.6 inches at Blue Hill Observatory in Milton.|Some of the higher snowfall totals, as reported by trained spotters and cooperative observers, included 13 inches in Ashfield, 12 inches in Greenfield, 11 inches in Goshen, 10 inches in Charlemont and Haverhill, 9 inches in Chester, Huntington, Pepperell, and Townsend, 8 inches in Turners Falls, Lowell, and Georgetown, and 6 inches in Holyoke, West Brookfield, Fitchburg, Hudson, Concord, and Andover.|Strong Northeast winds gusted as high as 50 mph from the Worcester Hills and Merrimack Valley to the South Coast, Cape Cod and the Islands. Nantucket Airport reported a peak sustained wind of 41 mph.

Rows: Arctic air spilled south across western Iowa after a snowstorm left 2 to 4 inches of snow over the area the previous day.  Lows dropped to 5 below to 15 below over the area and when combined with north winds around 10 mph...wind chill values fell to 20 below to 30 below zero.

Arctic air spread south across fresh snow that covered western Iowa this morning.  The cold air was ushered in on north winds of 10 to 15 mph.  When combined with actual low temperatures that fell to 10 below to 15 below zero, wind chill values of 20 below to 30 below zero were observed.  These bitter cold conditions lasted from around midnight until 1000 am.

Low pressure developed across the lower Mississippi river valley on the morning of the 13th and moved into the central Appalachians by the early morning hours of the 14th. During the early morning hours of the 14th, a coastal low quickly developed near the Delmarva peninsula and rapidly intensified, as it moved northeast across southeast Massachusetts and into the Gulf of Maine by the evening of the 14th.|Snow moved into southern Vermont around midnight on the 14th, then overspread the rest of Vermont during the early morning hours. Snow fell heavy at times from late morning through early afternoon in southern Vermont and early afternoon through early evening elsewhere, before dissipating during the night. Snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and brisk winds of 15 to 25 mph caused near whiteout conditions at times, along with considerable blowing and drifting of the snow, making roads nearly impassable. Further, temperatures in the single numbers above zero combined with these brisk winds created wind chill values of 10 degrees below zero or colder. |Snowfall totals ranged from 15 to 25 inches in the Connecticut river valley to 20 to 35 inches elsewhere across Vermont. The National Weather Service office in South Burlington set an all-time record 24 hour snowfall of 25.3 inches, breaking the old mark of 23.1 inches set on January 14, 1934. There were additional indirect injuries resulting from this storm, including vehicle accidents and cardiac arrests due to overexertion during snow removal. Snow removal operations took several days and up to a week in some urban communities. In addition, the weight of the heavy snowfall on some weaker roofs, resulted in the partial or total collapse of 20 or more barn roofs and the deaths of more than 100 cattle.

Arctic air spilled south across western Iowa after a snowstorm left 2 to 4 inches of snow over the area the previous day.  Lows dropped to 5 below to 15 below over the area and when combined with north winds around 10 mph...wind chill values fell to 20 below to 30 below zero.

Arctic air spread south across fresh snow that covered western Iowa this morning.  The cold air was ushered in on north winds of 10 to 15 mph.  When combined with actual low temperatures that fell to 5 below to 10 below zero, wind chill values of 20 below to 25 below zero were observed.  These bitter cold conditions lasted from around 400 am until 1000 am.

Rows: Light to moderate snowfall impacted the South Plains region of west Texas on Valentine's Day. The snow began during the pre-dawn hours of the 14th, and persisted intermittently through much of the evening hours. Minor snow accumulations that ranged between a dusting up to three inches were common, with a few localized higher amounts. |Up to four inches of snow accumulated at Farwell (Parmer County), but the long duration of light to moderate snowfall that led to the accumulation exceeded time requirements for local Heavy Snow/Winter Storm criteria.|The widespread winter weather resulted in at least 125 vehicle accidents across the region. More than 110 of the collisions occurred in Lubbock. Damages exceeded $325,000. No injuries were reported.||A list of reported snow accumulations are as follows: 4 inches at Farwell (Parmer County), 3 inches at Dimmitt (Castro County), 2 inches at Dickens (Dickens County), 2 inches at Lubbock (Lubbock County), 2 inches at Muleshoe (Bailey County), 2 inches at Plainview (Hale County), 2 inches at Tulia (Swisher County), 1 inch at Childress (Childress County), 1 inch at Floydada (Floyd County), 1 inch at Littlefield (Lamb County), 1 inch at Memphis (Hall County), 1 inch at Morton (Cochran County), and 1 inch at Silverton (Briscoe County).

Rows: Arctic air spilled south across western Iowa after a snowstorm left 2 to 4 inches of snow over the area the previous day.  Lows dropped to 5 below to 15 below over the area and when combined with north winds around 10 mph...wind chill values fell to 20 below to 30 below zero.

Arctic air spread south across fresh snow that covered western Iowa this morning.  The cold air was ushered in on north winds of 10 to 15 mph.  When combined with actual low temperatures that fell to around 10 below zero, wind chill values of 20 below to 25 below zero were observed.  These bitter cold conditions lasted from around 500 am until 800 am.

Rows: Rapidly intensifying low pressure across southern New England during the 14th...lifted north across the Gulf of Maine and eastern Maine during the night of the 14th and morning of the 15th. Snow developed and expanded north across the region during the 14th...becoming heavy at times. Across Downeast areas...enough warm air was drawn north to change the precipitation to sleet and freezing rain with a transition to all rain for a time along the immediate coast. Strong winds also affected the Downeast coast...where wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph were reported. Some trees and power lines were toppled along the coast leading to power outages. Storm total snowfall across Downeast Maine generally ranged from 6 to 10 inches...with 1/2 to 1 inch of sleet and varying amounts of ice accumulation from freezing rain. Rows: Low pressure strengthened rapidly as it tracked from the mid Atlantic coast to Cape Cod. The season's first winter storm brought snow, sleet and freezing rain to interior sections of Massachusetts and heavy rain with strong northeast winds along the coast.|Snow began in western Massachusetts during the evening of the 13th and reached the coast by midnight. Milder air coming off the ocean caused the snow to change to sleet and freezing rain during the day on the 14th from the Mass Turnpike region into the Merrimack Valley, and to all rain in greater Boston and points south. Temperatures fell sharply late in the day and during the evening, causing a flash freeze and icy travel conditions. Precipitation changed back to snow before ending around midnight on the 15th.|The highest snowfall totals, on the order of 6 to 12 inches, were observed from the east slopes of the Berskhires to the Route 2 corridor and into the Merrimack Valley. Although snowfall totals only averaged 2 to 5 inches farther to the south, the combination of snow and ice resulted in hazardous travel conditions. Dozens of minor accidents were reported.|Official snowfall totals included 9.8 inches at Worcester Airport, 2.5 inches at Logan Airport in Boston, 2.1 inches at the National Weather Service office in Taunton, and 1.6 inches at Blue Hill Observatory in Milton.|Some of the higher snowfall totals, as reported by trained spotters and cooperative observers, included 13 inches in Ashfield, 12 inches in Greenfield, 11 inches in Goshen, 10 inches in Charlemont and Haverhill, 9 inches in Chester, Huntington, Pepperell, and Townsend, 8 inches in Turners Falls, Lowell, and Georgetown, and 6 inches in Holyoke, West Brookfield, Fitchburg, Hudson, Concord, and Andover.|Strong Northeast winds gusted as high as 50 mph from the Worcester Hills and Merrimack Valley to the South Coast, Cape Cod and the Islands. Nantucket Airport reported a peak sustained wind of 41 mph.

Rows: Disturbances embedded in a moist northwest flow brought snow and windy conditions to the central and northern mountains of western Colorado.

Rows: In the wake of the February 13th and 14th nor'easter, unseasonably cold air was drawn southward into Pennsylvania on gusty west to northwest winds on the 15th and 16th. From upper Bucks County northward through the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos, morning low temperature were mainly in the positive single numbers both days. Wind chill factors reached as low as 20 degrees below zero on the Pocono Plateau and between zero and 10 degrees below zero elsewhere. The unseasonably cold weather led to pipes being burst at the Snowshoe Condominium in Mount Pocono. One family was displaced. Actual low temperatures included 3 degrees below zero at the F.E. Walter Dam (Carbon County), 1 degree in Mount Pocono (Monroe County), 4 degrees in Perkasie (Bucks County), 6 degrees in Springtown (Bucks County), 7 degrees at the Lehigh Valley International Airport, 8 degrees in Hamburg (Berks County), 10 degrees in Easton (Northampton County) and 11 degrees in Reading (Berks County).

Rows: A strong upper level jet stream over northern Colorado, coupled with a passing weather disturbance, brought a one-two punch of heavy snow and strong winds to areas in and near the Front Range.  In the North Central Mountains, a peak wind gust to 106 mph was recorded atop Berthoud Pass.  U.S. Highway 40 was closed temporarily at Berthoud Pass, and between Kremmling and Steamboat Springs, due to an increased avalanche danger.  One avalanche knocked a state highway vehicle off the road near Berthoud Pass.  At Winter Park, the ski area was forced to shut down when strong winds toppled several trees.  Elsewhere, two sections of Interstate 70 were closed including a 60-mile stretch from east of Vail to west of Evergreen.  U.S. Highway 6 over Loveland Pass, and U.S. Highway 285, over Kenosha Pass, were also closed.  The American Red Cross set up temporary shelters in Granby, Fraser and Silverthorne for stranded travelers.  Storm totals in the high country ranged from 7 to 18 inches.|Very intense winds also developed in the Front Range Foothills, Urban Corridor and Northeast Plains.  At the National Wind Technology Center, the peak wind gust topped out at 101 mph.  In and near the Front Range Foothills, the wind stirred up intense ground blizzards which resulted in several road closures.  State Highway 93, between Golden and Boulder was closed for much of the day.  In addition, State Highways 72 and 128, from Indiana St. and McCaslin Blvd. respectively, were closed due to near zero visibilities in blowing and drifting snow.  East of Interstate 25, peak wind gusts to around 60 mph were recorded.  At Denver International Airport, blowing debris cracked the front and side windshields of 14 airplanes within a three hour period.  In all, three airlines were impacted in the incident.

Rows: A strong upper level jet stream over northern Colorado, coupled with a passing weather disturbance, brought a one-two punch of heavy snow and strong winds to areas in and near the Front Range.  In the North Central Mountains, a peak wind gust to 106 mph was recorded atop Berthoud Pass.  U.S. Highway 40 was closed temporarily at Berthoud Pass, and between Kremmling and Steamboat Springs, due to an increased avalanche danger.  One avalanche knocked a state highway vehicle off the road near Berthoud Pass.  At Winter Park, the ski area was forced to shut down when strong winds toppled several trees.  Elsewhere, two sections of Interstate 70 were closed including a 60-mile stretch from east of Vail to west of Evergreen.  U.S. Highway 6 over Loveland Pass, and U.S. Highway 285, over Kenosha Pass, were also closed.  The American Red Cross set up temporary shelters in Granby, Fraser and Silverthorne for stranded travelers.  Storm totals in the high country ranged from 7 to 18 inches.|Very intense winds also developed in the Front Range Foothills, Urban Corridor and Northeast Plains.  At the National Wind Technology Center, the peak wind gust topped out at 101 mph. Deep low pressure in the Northern Plains and high pressure in the Great Basin combined to create a strong pressure gradient across Wyoming. Sustained wind of 40 to 50 mph with gusts of 60 to 70 mph were common. A peak peak gust of 90 mph was recorded on Chief Joseph Pass in Park County. Other notable peak gusts included 71 mph at Buffalo and 66 mph at both Riverton Regional Airport and Beaver Rim.

In the wake of the February 13th and 14th nor'easter, unseasonably cold air was drawn southward into Pennsylvania on gusty west to northwest winds on the 15th and 16th. From upper Bucks County northward through the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos, morning low temperature were mainly in the positive single numbers both days. Wind chill factors reached as low as 20 degrees below zero on the Pocono Plateau and between zero and 10 degrees below zero elsewhere. The unseasonably cold weather led to pipes being burst at the Snowshoe Condominium in Mount Pocono. One family was displaced. Actual low temperatures included 3 degrees below zero at the F.E. Walter Dam (Carbon County), 1 degree in Mount Pocono (Monroe County), 4 degrees in Perkasie (Bucks County), 6 degrees in Springtown (Bucks County), 7 degrees at the Lehigh Valley International Airport, 8 degrees in Hamburg (Berks County), 10 degrees in Easton (Northampton County) and 11 degrees in Reading (Berks County).

Rows: A strong low pressure system moved across the northern Plains and produced heavy upslope snowfall across the Wyoming Black Hills and the Bear Lodge Mountains. Six to 15 inches of snow fell across much of the area, with the highest amounts around Four Corners. Gusty winds produced blowing and drifting snow and reduced visibilities to a quarter of a mile or less at times.

The following wind reports were received: 60 mph gust 3NNE Wilsall, 63 mph gust in Judith Gap, 81 mph gust 3W Fishtail(Fishtail RAWS), 59 mph gust in Pine Creek, 60 mph gust in Harlowton, 62 mph gust 14ESE Musselshell(Kilo RAWS), 80 mph gust 6ENE Livingston, 68 mph gust in Rapelje, 62 mph gust 15SSE Roundup, 60 mph gust 5ENE Lame Deer, 46 mph sustained winds 2ESE Alzada, 48 mph sustained winds 2NW Rock Springs, 55 mph sustained winds 11W Livingston, 43 mph sustained winds 18E Billings, 44 mph sustained winds in Billings, 87 mph wind gust 9ESE Chico(Wicked Creek RAWS), 61 mph gust in Miles City, 82 mph gust 21E Warren(Hillsboro RAWS), 50 mph sustained winds 8S Wyola, 64 mph gust 8S Bridger(Deer Mountain RAWS) and a 66 mph gust 8S Wyola.

Deep low pressure in the Northern Plains and high pressure in the Great Basin combined to create a strong pressure gradient across Wyoming. Sustained wind of 40 to 50 mph with gusts of 60 to 70 mph were common. A peak peak gust of 90 mph was recorded on Chief Joseph Pass in Park County. Other notable peak gusts included 71 mph at Buffalo and 66 mph at both Riverton Regional Airport and Beaver Rim.

A strong low pressure system moved across the northern Plains, producing very strong winds and significant amounts of upslope snowfall across the northern and central Black Hills. The heaviest snow developed from Cheyenne Crossing to Lead and Deadwood, where 10 to 20 inches fell, with five to ten inches of snow across the rest of the northern and central Black Hills. Gusty winds produced blowing and drifting snow and reduced visibilities to a quarter of a mile or less at times.

A persistent northwest to west flow following the winter storm on February 13th and 14th culminated in blow-out tides around the times of low tide from the late morning of the 16th into the early morning of the 17th. The lowest tides in northern New Jersey occurred around Noon EST on the 16th, and in southern New Jersey and in Delaware Bay early on the 17th. The new moon assisted, because spring tides cause the biggest differences in water levels between high and low tides. The low tide at Sandy Hook (Monmouth County) reached 2.67 feet below mean lower low water; at Atlantic City (Atlantic County) reached 2.58 feet below mean lower low water and in Cape May (Cape May County) reached 2.37 feet below mean lower low water. Blowout tides start at 1.8 feet below mean lower low water. The west flow subsided late in the day on the 17th and on the 18th.

A fast moving upper level storm system crossed the area during the afternoon and evening. The precipitation began briefly as freezing rain and sleet then changed quickly to snow. Temperatures fell and winds increased with the changeover to snow. This caused numerous accidents and a few indirect injuries as drivers had difficulty maneuvering on the icy roads. Snowfall totals were generally two inches or less.|However, two to four inches were reported in a few spots along and either side of Interstate 70. Isolated spots in north central Kansas reported up to a half inch of sleet and snow.

A persistent northwest to west flow following the winter storm on February 13th and 14th culminated in blow-out tides around the times of low tide during the late afternoon and early evening of the 16th and the morning of the 17th. The lowest tides occurred on the morning of the 17th. The new moon assisted, because spring tides cause the biggest differences in water levels between high and low tides. Low tide in Philadelphia (Pennsylvania) reached 2.3 feet below mean lower low water. Blowout tides start at 1.8 feet below mean lower low water. The west flow subsided later in the day on the 17th.

A winter storm moving to the south of the region brought very strong winds to south-central Nebraska. Accompanying the winds was some snow, especially east of Grand Island. The mixture of snow and wind caused very poor visibilities for a few hours. The worst visibilities were reported along US Highway 81 between Hebron and Columbus. Visibilities in this corridor were near zero at times in open country. The highest wind gusts, 59 mph, were at Ord and Grand Island. A 58 mph wind gust was reported at Aurora and Hastings reported a sustained wind over 40 mph between 9 and 10 pm.  No major damage was caused by the winds.

Rows: A trade wind regime brought wintry weather to the mountain summits on Maui and the Big Island of Hawaii, and high surf of 6 to 9 feet along the east-facing shores of Niihau, Kauai, Oahu, Molokai, Maui, and the Big Island.  No serious property damage or injuries were reported.

Freezing rain fell over the summits of Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa on the Big Island of Hawaii.  The road to the summits was closed for a time on the 17th of February until the ice on the road surfaces melted.

This clipper type system spread a 2-4 inch swath of snow across most of southern Illinois. The highest amounts were in the Lower Wabash Valley and along Interstate 64, where 3 to 4 inches were common. Only around an inch fell in the Mississippi River counties, including Carbondale.

A vigorous storm system moved from western Iowa southeast across the Mid Mississippi Valley into eastern Kentucky. This clipper type system produced about an inch of snow in Perry and Cape Girardeau Counties. The wet snowfall caused some minor accidents. A sport utility vehicle rolled over on Interstate 55 in Cape Girardeau. There were no injuries, but the northbound lanes were briefly closed at mile marker 101 while the vehicle was pulled out of the median. A couple of injury accidents were reported in or very close to Cape Girardeau County on county roads. Both accidents occurred before sunrise on the 17th.

A vigorous storm system moved from western Iowa southeast across the Mid Mississippi Valley into eastern Kentucky. This clipper type system spread a 1-3 inch swath of snow across parts of western Kentucky, mainly along and north of the Western Kentucky Parkway. The highest amounts were from Madisonville and Providence eastward, where about 3 inches fell. Generally one to two inches fell elsewhere, including Henderson and Owensboro. The snowfall resulted in mostly minor accidents and slide-offs. Owensboro police worked 13 minor wrecks, while Daviess County deputies worked eight minor wrecks.

Dry weather conditions in two locations helped sustain fires that burned more than 1000 acres in each case.

A fire scorched 1500 acres of mainly brush in an area 6 miles south/southeast of Waikoloa on the west side of the Big Island of Hawaii.   Mamalahoa Highway was closed for a few hours by the fire, as was one lane of Waikoloa Road, south of Kamuela.  Traffic became snarled under the circumstances.  The cause of the blaze was unknown.  No homes were evacuated, and no structures were threatened.  There were no significant injuries.|

After 10:00 am Sunday 18 February 2007, 2 bodies were found and 1 lost at sea along the mouth of Aoa village harbor which lies to the north to northeast of Tutuila Island of American Samoa. The youngest of the deceased was seen alive Saturday afternoon as he was yelling for help in the ocean while swimming.  2 residents of Aoa village jumped in the water and tried to rescue this young male. A local rescue team and divers responded to this incident and conducted a search, but were unsuccessful Saturday evening.  2 bodies were found the next day while the other remains missing.|Seas were 3 to 5 feet on this day, and all weather equipments were operating normally.|This will be the first drowning incident for American Samoa in 2007.

A modified Arctic air mass remained over the region during mid-February.  Meanwhile, a weak upper disturbance passed over the cold air.  This resulted in light precipitation, mostly in the form of light snow, across the far northern counties of Georgia.  Accumulations of snow were generally confined to areas north and east of an Ellijay, to Dawsonville, to Dahlonega line.  Much of the snow melted within a few hours of falling as temperatures remained near or just above the freezing mark throughout the event.

Rows: Another strong northwest flow between a high pressure system building in from Canada and a low pressure system deepening over the Canadian Maritimes brought another unseasonably cold shot of air into northwestern New Jersey. Morning wind chills on the 19th were between zero and 10 degrees below zero. Actual low temperatures were in the positive single numbers. Since this occurred on President's Day, it did not have the same effect as a typical weekday day. Low temperatures included zero at High Point (Sussex County), 5 degrees in Randolph (Morris County), 6 degrees in Hope (Warren County), 7 degrees in Andover (Sussex County), 8 degrees in Parsippany (Morris County) and Pequest (Somerset County) and 9 degrees in Basking Ridge (Somerset County), Phillipsburg (Warren County) and Wertsville (Hunterdon County).

Rows: Dry weather conditions in two locations helped sustain fires that burned more than 1000 acres in each case.

Seven people had to be evacuated when a brush fire moved closed to their homes about two-and-a-half miles east/southeast of Lahaina in West Maui.  The fire eventually blackened 1350 acres, and destroyed one small structure and several vehicles.  Damage estimates were not available.  There were no significant injuries.  The cause of the fire was under investigation, though fire officials believed it was intentionally set.|

Rows: An arctic airmass the first two weeks of February resulted in sub-freezing temperatures, both for daily highs and lows.  The cold spell was followed by a rapid warm-up and resulted in ice jams and flooding across south-central Nebraska.  Ice jam flooding began on February 20th and lasted until February 27th. Flooding affected the Cedar River, Mud Creek, Sappa Creek, Wood River, Loup River, and the North, South and Middle Loup River branches.  Due to the ice jams, water overflowed the banks of the rivers and caused low land flooding. Water flowed over the Burlington Northern railroad tracks and state highway 2 between Ravenna and Sweetwater near the confluence of the Mud Creek and the South Loup River. Water also affected county roads adjacent to the rivers and creeks.

A prolonged cold spell in late January and early February caused ice over a foot thick to form on slow moving streams and rivers in eastern Nebraska.  When temperatures climbed into the 40s and 50s toward the end of February, snow melt and ice break-up caused significant ice jams on some creeks and rivers across the region.  Those most affected included the Loup River west of Columbus, the Cedar River near Cedar Rapids, the Platte River from Schuyler to the Sarpy and Cass county border, the Elkhorn River from just southeast of Norfolk to near Crowell and Bazile, Ponca and Bow Creeks across Knox county.

Rows: The first severe weather episode of 2007 occurred across southeast Missouri during the evening.  A cold front pressed southeast across the region during the afternoon as a wave of low pressure shifted east along the front into the Ozarks of northern Arkansas.  Southerly flow ahead of the low brought warm moist air northward as temperatures reached the 60s.  The atmosphere destabilized enough by late afternoon to allow for the development of thunderstorms over southeast Missouri. These storms were prolific hail producers.

Rows: The first severe weather episode of 2007 occurred across southern Illinois during the evening.  A cold front pressed southeast across the region during the afternoon as a wave of low pressure shifted east along the front into the Ozarks of northern Arkansas.  Southerly flow ahead of the low brought warm moist air northward as temperatures reached the 60s.  The atmosphere destabilized enough by late afternoon to allow for the development of thunderstorms over southeast Missouri. These storms were prolific hail producers as they crossed into southern Illinois.

Rows: A prolonged cold spell in late January and early February caused ice over a foot thick to form on slow moving streams and rivers in eastern Nebraska.  When temperatures climbed into the 40s and 50s toward the end of February, snow melt and ice break-up caused significant ice jams on some creeks and rivers across the region.  Those most affected included the Loup River west of Columbus, the Cedar River near Cedar Rapids, the Platte River from Schuyler to the Sarpy and Cass county border, the Elkhorn River from just southeast of Norfolk to near Crowell and Bazile, Ponca and Bow Creeks across Knox county.

Ice jam flooding was reported on Ponca Creek near Verdel, on Bazile Creek east southeast of Niobrara, Bow Creek near Wynot and Verdigre Creek north of Verdigre.  The jams on Bazile and Ponca Creeks were each at least a mile long at one time, and caused flooding which closed several county roads and flooded farmland in the area.  The jam east of Niobrara also closed Highway 12 from 2 am on 2/22 until 430 am 2/23.

Details.Description: Ice jam flooding was reported on Ponca Creek near Verdel, on Bazile Creek east southeast of Niobrara, Bow Creek near Wynot and Verdigre Creek north of Verdigre. The jam east of Niobrara also closed Highway 12 from 2 am on 2/22 until 430 am 2/23.

Rows: A moderate Low pressure system persisted in the Central Gulf of Alaska on Wednesday 2/21. Due to arctic High pressure over the Northern Yukon, a strong surface pressure gradient formed forcing cold dry air to toward the south for the inner channels. The Low caused moist air to ride up over this cold air as the low center started to move SE on Wednesday evening. The arctic front remained over the Central Panhandle to cause heavy snow into the morning of Thursday, 2/22.

A trained spotter 9 miles south of Petersburg measured 8.8 inches in 12 hours ending at 0707 AKST 2/22. The augmented AWOS at Wrangell had 17.0 inches new snow for 24 hours ending at 1500 AKST 2/22. A trained spotter measured 16.0 inches of new snowfall for 12 hours ending at 0600 2/22. Zone 26 was buried.

Rows: Strong northwest winds gusting to 39 to 45 knots (45 to 52 mph) affected much of south-central and southeast Wisconsin during the pre-dawn hours of February 22nd.  Many, small tree limbs were knocked down, with some of them hitting power lines.  This resulted in scattered power outages.  The highest two wind gusts were 45 knots (52 mph) at both Milwaukee Mitchell Field (Milwaukee Co.) and at a Milwaukee TV-6 school network site in Grafton (Ozaukee Co.).  Otherwise all other maximum wind gusts were in the 39 to 42 knot range (45 to 48 mph).

A prolonged cold spell in late January and early February caused ice over a foot thick to form on slow moving streams and rivers in eastern Nebraska.  When temperatures climbed into the 40s and 50s toward the end of February, snow melt and ice break-up caused significant ice jams on some creeks and rivers across the region.  Those most affected included the Loup River west of Columbus, the Cedar River near Cedar Rapids, the Platte River from Schuyler to the Sarpy and Cass county border, the Elkhorn River from just southeast of Norfolk to near Crowell and Bazile, Ponca and Bow Creeks across Knox county.
Ice jam flooding along the Elkhorn River closed county roads and surrounded 4 houses west of Stanton near the Madison county line.

A prolonged cold spell in late January and early February caused ice over a foot thick to form on slow moving streams and rivers in eastern Nebraska.  When temperatures climbed into the 40s and 50s toward the end of February, snow melt and ice break-up caused significant ice jams on some creeks and rivers across the region.  Those most affected included the Loup River west of Columbus, the Cedar River near Cedar Rapids, the Platte River from Schuyler to the Sarpy and Cass county border, the Elkhorn River from just southeast of Norfolk to near Crowell and Bazile, Ponca and Bow Creeks across Knox county.

A cold Pacific storm system moved across central California from the morning of the 22nd until the morning of the 23rd. Snow fell as low as the Sierra Nevada foothills, with up to 6 inches of snow falling in Mariposa County tapering off sharply to the south, with less than 2 inches being reported in Tulare County. The largest amount over the higher elevations was 22 inches at Lodgepole (6735 feet msl). Snow also fell across the Kern County mountains, closing State Highway 58 through the Tehachapi Pass. Strong winds developed in the wake of the system across the Kern County desert into the evening of the 23rd.

A low pressure system over the Great Lakes intensified as it moved southeast across central New York and northeast Pennsylvania on the 22nd. Initially, the air was mild ahead of the storm. Ice jams on the Elkhorn River caused extensive flooding of lowland farmlands from southeast of Wisner to southeast of West Point.  At first the flooding was very unpredictable and unstable due to the forming and breaking up of the jams, but eventually two large jams became established in Cuming county about 3 miles apart near West Point. The flood waters from these ice jams covered at least 1000 acres of farmland and closed many county roads in the area.  In addition...a 15 mile stretch of Highway 275 southeast of Wisner was closed at one time or another with a 5 mile section of the Highway closed for a large part of this period. Rows: A widespread and crippling ice/snow storm affected eastern Iowa, northwest and western Illinois, and extreme northeast Missouri on February 24, 2007. This massive ice storm was the worst to affect the region since January 22-23, 1965. Ice accumulations of around one inch were common, with some reports to near two inches! To make matters worse, east winds gusting over 50 mph, combined with the heavy ice accumulation, brought down numerous tree branches and power lines, along with several thousand power poles. There were even whole trees crashing down from the weight of the ice. Widespread power outages occurred, affecting over 180,000 people, which lasted more than a week in some of the rural areas. Many shelters were opened to accommodate those without power. In the northern portions of the region in the colder air, snow was the problem. Accumulations of up to 7 inches occurred, with strong winds combining to create blizzard conditions. Considering the magnitude of the storm, remarkably no direct deaths were reported.

Very strong Theta-e advection took place over Iowa during the day on the 23rd as a storm system developed over the front range of Colorado and Wyoming.  Low level winds increased to over 50 kts during the day, drawing in considerable moisture north across the colder air at the surface.  I was located north of a surface warm front.  Elevated thunderstorms developed during the day and pushed northeast across the state.  Instability parameters were limited, however 500 J/kg of shear was available in the most unstable layer, with 100 J/kg of that in the -10 to -30 C layer.  The effective zero to 3 km shear was around 25 kts.  Most of the thunderstorms produced one quarter to one half inch diameter hail and a considerable amount of sleet.  There was enough to cover the ground in many places.  One of the storms became severe in Webster County and produced three quarter inch diameter hail.  As the thunderstorms moved through the Cedar Falls area, lightning struck a house there causing a small dormer fire.

Rows: A powerful winter storm moved from Kansas to the lower Great Lakes, producing a combination of freezing rain, sleet and heavy snow, which virtually paralyzed northeast Iowa. Widespread power outages and tree damage were caused by ice accumulations of 1 to 2 inches. Especially hard hit were locations from around Oelwein (Fayette County) to New Hampton (Chicksaw County) to Osage (Mitchell County). Several roads had downed power lines across them and in fact, thousands of power poles were downed due to ice. Heavy snow also accompanied the storm. Accumulations ranged from 6 to 18 inches, with highest totals near the Minnesota-Iowa border. Some of the highest totals included 18.8 inches near Decorah (Winneshiek County) and 16.4 inches at Dorchester (Allamakee County). Thousands of people were without power for several days and emergency shelters were provided to accomodate those needing assistance. Travel was dangerous or impossible throughout northeast Iowa.
A cold and moist low pressure system swept east across the area and produced significant snowfall and gusty winds.
Five to six inches of snow fell across the area.  Wind gusts of 20 to 30 mph caused blowing and drifting snow.

Rows: A powerful winter storm moved from Kansas to the lower Great Lakes. This storm produced a combination of significant heavy snow, sleet and ice accumulations, which virtually paralyzed southeast Minnesota. Near the Mississippi River, snow accumulations totaled 20 to 26 inches, with an isolated report of 29.5 inches near Winona (Winona County). Further west, ice accumulations of 3/4 inch to 1.5 inches affected areas mainly southwest of Rochester (Olmsted County), including Austin (Mower County) and Stewartville (Olmsted County). Adams in Mower County was especially hard hit with thick glaze ice, numerous power poles and trees downed.  A heavy glaze of ice in these locations caused power outages. Travel was dangerous or impossible througout southeast Minnesota.

Heavy snow was widespread across southwest Wisconsin, as a powerful winter storm moved from Kansas to the lower Great Lakes. Hardest hit were areas near the Mississippi River from near La Crosse (La Crosse County) to Galesville (Trempealeau County) and Fountain City (Buffalo County). Snow accumulations in these areas totaled 20 to 25 inches. In fact, La Crosse established an all-time record three day snowfall total of 21 inches. In addition to the heavy snow, ice accumulations of 1/4 to 1/2 inch impacted areas generally around the Wisconsin River and southward. Travel was dangerous or nearly impossible over all of southwest Wisconsin.

A winter storm (first of two rounds) consisting of heavy snow with some sleet and freezing rain mixed in, left behind 6 to 8.5 inches of accumulations over several south-central and southeast Wisconsin counties.  Additionally, there were frequent wind gusts to around 25 mph which resulted in a fair amount of blowing and drifing of the new snow.  The greatest snow accumulatins occurred north of a line from Madison (Dane Co.) to Brown Deer (Miwaukee Co.).  Maximum amounts in each affected county include 8 inches in Brown Deer, just over 6 inches in extreme northwest Waukesha County, 7.5 inches near Lake Mills (Jefferson Co.), 8.3 inches south of Middleton (Dane Co.), 8.5 inches in Saukville (Ozaukee Co.), 7.7 inches northwest of Beaver Dam (Dodge Co.), 8 inches in the Wisconsin Dells area (Columbia Co.), 8 inches in the Lake Delton area (Sauk Co.), 7.4 inches near Oxford (Marquette Co.), 8.5 inches between Berlin and Green Lake (Green Lake Co.), 8 inches just west of Ripon (Fond du Lac Co.), and about 6.5 inches in extreme southwest Sheboygan County.  A 34-year-old man died (indirectly-related) in a vehicle accident on a slippery road in the Town of Springfield (Dane Co.) Friday night.  The roof of an abandoned building in McFarland (Dane Co.) collapsed Friday night due to the weight of the heavy, wet snow. |Synoptically, this winter storm was the result of a strong upper-level short wave trough moving northeast through Wisconsin with plenty of warm-air advection and moisture advection in the low to mid levels of the atmosphere.  Some rumbles of thunder were reported as well.  Lesser amounts of snow, in the 3 to less than 6 inch range, fell near the Illinois border.  Further northwest in the La Crosse area, 12 to 14 inches of snow were measured.

A powerful winter storm moved from Kansas to the lower Great Lakes. This storm produced a combination of significant heavy snow, sleet and ice accumulations, which virtually paralyzed southeast Minnesota. Near the Mississippi River, snow accumulations totaled 20 to 26 inches, with an isolated report of 29.5 inches near Winona (Winona County). Further west, ice accumulations of 3/4 inch to 1.5 inches affected areas mainly southwest of Rochester (Olmsted County), including Austin (Mower County) and Stewartville (Olmsted County). Adams in Mower County was especially hard hit with thick glaze ice, numerous power poles and trees downed.  A heavy glaze of ice in these locations caused power outages. Travel was dangerous or impossible througout southeast Minnesota.

Very strong Theta-e advection took place over Iowa during the day on the 23rd as a storm system developed over the front range of Colorado and Wyoming.  Low level winds increased to over 50 kts during the day, drawing in considerable moisture north across the colder air at the surface.  I was located north of a surface warm front.  Elevated thunderstorms developed during the day and pushed northeast across the state.  Instability parameters were limited, however 500 J/kg of shear was available in the most unstable layer, with 100 J/kg of that in the -10 to -30 C layer.  The effective zero to 3 km shear was around 25 kts.  Most of the thunderstorms produced one quarter to one half inch diameter hail and a considerable amount of sleet.  There was enough to cover the ground in many places.  One of the storms became severe in Webster County and produced three quarter inch diameter hail.  As the thunderstorms moved through the Cedar Falls area, lightning struck a house there causing a small dormer fire.

Rows: A strong area of low pressure tracking across the central plains brought widespread snowfall to parts of central and much of northeast South Dakota. The precipitation initially began as freezing rain and sleet late in the evening of the 23rd as it lifted across the area through the morning of the 24th. The freezing rain and sleet then changed over to snow during the morning hours of the 24th. Thundersnow also occurred at some locations across the area. Snowfall amounts of 6 to 15 inches had occurred as the storm ended. With the initial slippery roads from the freezing rain and then the heavy snow, travel conditions became very difficult. The State Emergency Management, Highway Patrol, and Department of Transportation issued a travel advisory for no travel for Interstate-90 and many highways in central South Dakota. There were numerous accidents along the interstate. Some snowfall amounts included, 9 inches at Bryant and Webster, 10 inches at Toronto, Roy Lake, and Garden City, 11 inches at Faulkton, 12 inches at Watertown, and 15 inches at Clear Lake.

A powerful storm system moved through the upper midwest in late February, and brought heavy snow to much of northeast Minnesota with localized blizzard conditions along the north shore of Lake Superior. The snow began late on the 23rd in the Cass and Brainerd Lakes area, and ended on the evening of the 25th. Snowfall of 12 to 14 inches occured at the head of Lake Superior from Two Harbors to Cloquet, as well as across the Cass and Brainerd Lakes area, through southern Aitkin County and into western Pine County. Areas from the Iron Range to northern and eastern areas of the arrowhead received less than 2 inches. In addition to the heavy snow, blizzard conditions occured across the north shore during the early morning hours of the 25th, with winds gusting 40 to 50 mph. Many churches in Duluth cancelled Sunday morning services because of blowing and drifting snow.

A strong upper level low pressure system moved from the Rockies on the 22nd, and across much of the Upper Midwest from the 23rd to the 25th. A large swath of heavy snow accompanied by sustained winds in the 15 to 20 mph range were noted across much of Central and South Central Minnesota. Some notable snow totals include: 17.5 inches at Hewitt (Todd County), 17.0 inches at New London (Kandiyohi County) and St. James (Watonwan County), 16.5 inches at 10 miles N of Mora (Kanabec County), 15.5 inches at Hutchinson (McLeod County), 14.0 inches at Albert Lea (Freeborn County), and 12.2 inches at Chanhassen (Carver County).

A strong area of low pressure tracking across the central plains brought widespread snowfall to parts of central and much of northeast South Dakota. The precipitation initially began as freezing rain and sleet late in the evening of the 23rd as it lifted across the area through the morning of the 24th. The freezing rain and sleet then changed over to snow during the morning hours of the 24th. Thundersnow also occurred at some locations across the area. Snowfall amounts of 6 to 15 inches had occurred as the storm ended. With the initial slippery roads from the freezing rain and then the heavy snow, travel conditions became very difficult. The State Emergency Management, Highway Patrol, and Department of Transportation issued a travel advisory for no travel for Interstate-90 and many highways in central South Dakota. There were numerous accidents along the interstate. Some snowfall amounts included, 9 inches at Bryant and Webster, 10 inches at Toronto, Roy Lake, and Garden City, 11 inches at Faulkton, 12 inches at Watertown, and 15 inches at Clear Lake.

A powerful storm system moved through the upper midwest in late February, and brought heavy snow to much of northeast Minnesota with localized blizzard conditions along the north shore of Lake Superior. The snow began late on the 23rd in the Cass and Brainerd Lakes area, and ended on the evening of the 25th. Snowfall of 12 to 14 inches occured at the head of Lake Superior from Two Harbors to Cloquet, as well as across the Cass and Brainerd Lakes area, through southern Aitkin County and into western Pine County. Areas from the Iron Range to northern and eastern areas of the arrowhead received less than 2 inches. In addition to the heavy snow, blizzard conditions occured across the north shore during the early morning hours of the 25th, with winds gusting 40 to 50 mph. Many churches in Duluth cancelled Sunday morning services because of blowing and drifting snow.

Outflow from decaying thunderstorms brought wind damage within the city of Herington. A large locust tree was blown onto a truck. A newly constructed metal carport that was staked to the ground was lifted and rotated 180 degrees before landing some 30 feet away. A metal storage shed was blown away from one property. The shed slammed into a gas meter rupturing it. Shingles were torn from roofs and a large plate glass window was blown out of a local business.

A powerful storm system moved through the upper midwest in late February, and brought heavy snow to portions of northwest Wisconsin. The snow began falling during the evening of the 24th, with some ice and sleet mixed in at the beginning. The heaviest snow fell during the morning of the 25th. Blizzard conditions were felt during the early morning hours of the 25th, as winds gusted to over 40 mph along the south shore of Lake Superior from the Bayfield Peninsula to Superior. On the back side of the low, winds turned northerly, with lake effect snow continuing across the south shore of Lake Superior. The snow finally ended during the evening of the 25th. Snow totals ranged from 6 to 10 inches, with the heaviest occuring over the Bayfield Peninsula, over towards Superior, as well as the upper St. Croix River Valley.

A major winter storm affected Iowa through the 24th and 25th of February.  A powerful upper low moved onto the west coast during the middle of the week, and advanced east through the Rockies during the end of the week.  Strong warm air advection took place over the top of a shallow polar airmass that was in place over Iowa.  The east-southeasterly flow at the surface drew cool and dry air into the state from the east, setting the stage for a significant ice storm.  The main area of precipitation overspread the state during the early morning hours of the 24th and persisted through much of the 25th.  Initially, very warm air aloft meant that the precipitation fell in the form of freezing rain and sleet.  The central and northeast sections of the CWA were most effected with the ice as the southwest warmed to just above freezing.  Ice accumulations ranged from around one quarter of an inch or so along a Carroll to Centerville line, to between one half and on inch over the northeast part of the CWA in the Waterloo, Tama, Marshalltown, to south of Mason City areas.  Widespread tree and power line damage was reported across much of the northeast two thirds of the CWA.  Reports of 345 KV lines down were received from Tama and Black Hawk Couties.  During this time, easterly winds were blowing in the 20 to 40 MPH range, exacerbating the problem.  Tama County reported 75 miles of power lines down.  Butler County reported at least 250 power poles snapped already by the evening of the 24th.  At the height of the storm, at least 265,000 customers were without power.  Interstate Power and Light Company reported that 1000 miles of transmission line was down at one point and 2000 utility poles were snapped in their area covered by Alliant Energy.  MidAmerica Energy reported 360 miles of transmission line down and 1600 utility poles snapped in their area.  Final damage figures for the three utility entities involved in the ice storm were $70,000,000 damage to Alliant Energy equipment, $36,000,000 damage to MidAmerica Energy equipment, and $32,000,000 damage to Rural Electric Cooperative equipment.  These figures are statewide figures and therefore were not entirely within the Des Moines CWA.  The freezing rain changed over to sleet, and eventually snow late on the 24th into the 25th.  Six to twelve inches of snow was common across much of Iowa northwest of a Bedford, to Des Moines, to Grundy Center line.  Some of the heavier amounts include 11.5 inches at Algona in Kossuth County, and 10 inches at Dana in Greene County and Estherville in Emmet County.  Along with the snow, many areas reported occasional visibility near zero in blowing snow on the night of the 24th into the 25th.  Travel became very hazardous with many roads closed due to the combination of snow, blowing snow, fallen wires, and fallen trees.  Numerous activities were canceled on the 25th as well.  By the afternoon of the 25th, Iowa Governor Chet Culver had already given 60 counties the state disaster declaration by the afternoon following the storm.  Subsequently, 46 of the counties, mostly in northeast Iowa, received a Presidential Disaster Declaration.  Some of the hardest hit areas were in Poweshiek, Marshall, Tama, and Black Hawk Counties. Costs in the city of Waterloo, for example, were over $2,000,000 during the first week after the storm. This winter storm went into the books as one of the worst winter storms in many years.  Although ice storms are not documented all that well, this storm appears to be the worst ice storm in Iowa in the past 40 years due to the large areal extent of the storm.  Farther to the south and west the precipitation fell as rain.  Enough rain fell to cause some minor flooding on the Chariton and Middle Rivers.  The Middle River crested about a foot over flood state in Indianola, while the Chariton River crested a little over 2 feet over flood stage in Chariton.

The east-southeasterly flow at the surface drew cool and dry air into the state from the east, setting the stage for a significant ice storm.  The main area of precipitation overspread the state during the early morning hours of the 24th and persisted through much of the 25th.  Initially, very warm air aloft meant that the precipitation fell in the form of freezing rain and sleet.  The central and northeast sections of the CWA were most effected with the ice as the southwest warmed to just above freezing.  Ice accumulations ranged from around one quarter of an inch or so along a Carroll to Centerville line, to between one half and on inch over the northeast part of the CWA in the Waterloo, Tama, Marshalltown, to south of Mason City areas.  Widespread tree and power line damage was reported across much of the northeast two thirds of the CWA.  Reports of 345 KV lines down were received from Tama and Black Hawk Couties.  During this time, easterly winds were blowing in the 20 to 40 MPH range, exacerbating the problem.  Tama County reported 75 miles of power lines down.  Butler County reported at least 250 power poles snapped already by the evening of the 24th.  At the height of the storm, at least 265,000 customers were without power. The east-southeasterly flow at the surface drew cool and dry air into the state from the east, setting the stage for a significant ice storm.  The main area of precipitation overspread the state during the early morning hours of the 24th and persisted through much of the 25th.  Initially, very warm air aloft meant that the precipitation fell in the form of freezing rain and sleet.  The central and northeast sections of the CWA were most effected with the ice as the southwest warmed to just above freezing.  Ice accumulations ranged from around one quarter of an inch or so along a Carroll to Centerville line, to between one half and on inch over the northeast part of the CWA in the Waterloo, Tama, Marshalltown, to south of Mason City areas.  Widespread tree and power line damage was reported across much of the northeast two thirds of the CWA.  Reports of 345 KV lines down were received from Tama and Black Hawk Couties.  During this time, easterly winds were blowing in the 20 to 40 MPH range, exacerbating the problem.  Tama County reported 75 miles of power lines down.  Butler County reported at least 250 power poles snapped already by the evening of the 24th.  At the height of the storm, at least 265,000 customers were without power.  Interstate Power and Light Company reported that 1000 miles of transmission line was down at one point and 2000 utility poles were snapped in their area covered by Alliant Energy.  MidAmerica Energy reported 360 miles of transmission line down and 1600 utility poles snapped in their area.  Final damage figures for the three utility entities involved in the ice storm were $70,000,000 damage to Alliant Energy equipment, $36,000,000 damage to MidAmerica Energy equipment, and $32,000,000 damage to Rural Electric Cooperative equipment.  These figures are statewide figures and therefore were not entirely within the Des Moines CWA.  The freezing rain changed over to sleet, and eventually snow late on the 24th into the 25th.  Six to twelve inches of snow was common across much of Iowa northwest of a Bedford, to Des Moines, to Grundy Center line.  Some of the heavier amounts include 11.5 inches at Algona in Kossuth County, and 10 inches at Dana in Greene County and Estherville in Emmet County.  Along with the snow, many areas reported occasional visibility near zero in blowing snow on the night of the 24th into the 25th.  Travel became very hazardous with many roads closed due to the combination of snow, blowing snow, fallen wires, and fallen trees.  Numerous activities were canceled on the 25th as well.  By the afternoon of the 25th, Iowa Governor Chet Culver had already given 60 counties the state disaster declaration by the afternoon following the storm.  Subsequently, 46 of the counties, mostly in northeast Iowa, received a Presidential Disaster Declaration.  Some of the hardest hit areas were in Poweshiek, Marshall, Tama, and Black Hawk Counties. Costs in the city of Waterloo, for example, were over $2,000,000 during the first week after the storm. This winter storm went into the books as one of the worst winter storms in many years.  Although ice storms are not documented all that well, this storm appears to be the worst ice storm in Iowa in the past 40 years due to the large areal extent of the storm.  Farther to the south and west the precipitation fell as rain.  Enough rain fell to cause some minor flooding on the Chariton and Middle Rivers.  The Middle River crested about a foot over flood state in Indianola, while the Chariton River crested a little over 2 feet over flood stage in Chariton.

The main area of precipitation overspread the state during the early morning hours of the 24th and persisted through much of the 25th.  Initially, very warm air aloft meant that the precipitation fell in the form of freezing rain and sleet.  The central and northeast sections of the CWA were most effected with the ice as the southwest warmed to just above freezing.  Ice accumulations ranged from around one quarter of an inch or so along a Carroll to Centerville line, to between one half and on inch over the northeast part of the CWA in the Waterloo, Tama, Marshalltown, to south of Mason City areas.  Widespread tree and power line damage was reported across much of the northeast two thirds of the CWA.  Reports of 345 KV lines down were received from Tama and Black Hawk Couties.  During this time, easterly winds were blowing in the 20 to 40 MPH range, exacerbating the problem.  Tama County reported 75 miles of power lines down.  Butler County reported at least 250 power poles snapped already by the evening of the 24th.  At the height of the storm, at least 265,000 customers were without power.  Interstate Power and Light Company reported that 1000 miles of transmission line was down at one point and 2000 utility poles were snapped in their area covered by Alliant Energy.  MidAmerica Energy reported 360 miles of transmission line down and 1600 utility poles snapped in their area.  Final damage figures for the three utility entities involved in the ice storm were $70,000,000 damage to Alliant Energy equipment, $36,000,000 damage to MidAmerica Energy equipment, and $32,000,000 damage to Rural Electric Cooperative equipment.  These figures are statewide figures and therefore were not entirely within the Des Moines CWA.  The freezing rain changed over to sleet, and eventually snow late on the 24th into the 25th.  Six to twelve inches of snow was common across much of Iowa northwest of a Bedford, to Des Moines, to Grundy Center line.  Some of the heavier amounts include 11.5 inches at Algona in Kossuth County, and 10 inches at Dana in Greene County and Estherville in Emmet County.  Along with the snow, many areas reported occasional visibility near zero in blowing snow on the night of the 24th into the 25th.  Travel became very hazardous with many roads closed due to the combination of snow, blowing snow, fallen wires, and fallen trees.  Numerous activities were canceled on the 25th as well.  By the afternoon of the 25th, Iowa Governor Chet Culver had already given 60 counties the state disaster declaration by the afternoon following the storm.  Subsequently, 46 of the counties, mostly in northeast Iowa, received a Presidential Disaster Declaration.  Some of the hardest hit areas were in Poweshiek, Marshall, Tama, and Black Hawk Counties. Costs in the city of Waterloo, for example, were over $2,000,000 during the first week after the storm. This winter storm went into the books as one of the worst winter storms in many years.  Although ice storms are not documented all that well, this storm appears to be the worst ice storm in Iowa in the past 40 years due to the large areal extent of the storm.  Farther to the south and west the precipitation fell as rain.  Enough rain fell to cause some minor flooding on the Chariton and Middle Rivers.  The Middle River crested about a foot over flood state in Indianola, while the Chariton River crested a little over 2 feet over flood stage in Chariton.

The central and northeast sections of the CWA were most effected with the ice as the southwest warmed to just above freezing.  Ice accumulations ranged from around one quarter of an inch or so along a Carroll to Centerville line, to between one half and on inch over the northeast part of the CWA in the Waterloo, Tama, Marshalltown, to south of Mason City areas.  Widespread tree and power line damage was reported across much of the northeast two thirds of the CWA.  Reports of 345 KV lines down were received from Tama and Black Hawk Couties.  During this time, easterly winds were blowing in the 20 to 40 MPH range, exacerbating the problem.  Tama County reported 75 miles of power lines down.  Butler County reported at least 250 power poles snapped already by the evening of the 24th.  At the height of the storm, at least 265,000 customers were without power.  Interstate Power and Light Company reported that 1000 miles of transmission line was down at one point and 2000 utility poles were snapped in their area covered by Alliant Energy.  MidAmerica Energy reported 360 miles of transmission line down and 1600 utility poles snapped in their area.  Final damage figures for the three utility entities involved in the ice storm were $70,000,000 damage to Alliant Energy equipment, $36,000,000 damage to MidAmerica Energy equipment, and $32,000,000 damage to Rural Electric Cooperative equipment.  These figures are statewide figures and therefore were not entirely within the Des Moines CWA.  The freezing rain changed over to sleet, and eventually snow late on the 24th into the 25th.  Six to twelve inches of snow was common across much of Iowa northwest of a Bedford, to Des Moines, to Grundy Center line.  Some of the heavier amounts include 11.5 inches at Algona in Kossuth County, and 10 inches at Dana in Greene County and Estherville in Emmet County.  Along with the snow, many areas reported occasional visibility near zero in blowing snow on the night of the 24th into the 25th.  Travel became very hazardous with many roads closed due to the combination of snow, blowing snow, fallen wires, and fallen trees.  Numerous activities were canceled on the 25th as well.  By the afternoon of the 25th, Iowa Governor Chet Culver had already given 60 counties the state disaster declaration by the afternoon following the storm.  Subsequently, 46 of the counties, mostly in northeast Iowa, received a Presidential Disaster Declaration.  Some of the hardest hit areas were in Poweshiek, Marshall, Tama, and Black Hawk Counties. Although ice storms are not documented all that well, this storm appears to be the worst ice storm in Iowa in the past 40 years due to the large areal extent of the storm.  Farther to the south and west the precipitation fell as rain.  Enough rain fell to cause some minor flooding on the Chariton and Middle Rivers.  The Middle River crested about a foot over flood state in Indianola, while the Chariton River crested a little over 2 feet over flood stage in Chariton.

Ice accumulations ranged from around one quarter of an inch or so along a Carroll to Centerville line, to between one half and on inch over the northeast part of the CWA in the Waterloo, Tama, Marshalltown, to south of Mason City areas.  Widespread tree and power line damage was reported across much of the northeast two thirds of the CWA.  Reports of 345 KV lines down were received from Tama and Black Hawk Couties.  During this time, easterly winds were blowing in the 20 to 40 MPH range, exacerbating the problem.  Tama County reported 75 miles of power lines down.  Butler County reported at least 250 power poles snapped already by the evening of the 24th.  At the height of the storm, at least 265,000 customers were without power.  Interstate Power and Light Company reported that 1000 miles of transmission line was down at one point and 2000 utility poles were snapped in their area covered by Alliant Energy.  MidAmerica Energy reported 360 miles of transmission line down and 1600 utility poles snapped in their area.  Final damage figures for the three utility entities involved in the ice storm were $70,000,000 damage to Alliant Energy equipment, $36,000,000 damage to MidAmerica Energy equipment, and $32,000,000 damage to Rural Electric Cooperative equipment.  These figures are statewide figures and therefore were not entirely within the Des Moines CWA.  The freezing rain changed over to sleet, and eventually snow late on the 24th into the 25th.  Six to twelve inches of snow was common across much of Iowa northwest of a Bedford, to Des Moines, to Grundy Center line.  Some of the heavier amounts include 11.5 inches at Algona in Kossuth County, and 10 inches at Dana in Greene County and Estherville in Emmet County.  Along with the snow, many areas reported occasional visibility near zero in blowing snow on the night of the 24th into the 25th.  Travel became very hazardous with many roads closed due to the combination of snow, blowing snow, fallen wires, and fallen trees.  Numerous activities were canceled on the 25th as well.  By the afternoon of the 25th, Iowa Governor Chet Culver had already given 60 counties the state disaster declaration by the afternoon following the storm.  Subsequently, 46 of the counties, mostly in northeast Iowa, received a Presidential Disaster Declaration.  Some of the hardest hit areas were in Poweshiek, Marshall, Tama, and Black Hawk Counties. Costs in the city of Waterloo, for example, were over $2,000,000 during the first week after the storm. This winter storm went into the books as one of the worst winter storms in many years.  Although ice storms are not documented all that well, this storm appears to be the worst ice storm in Iowa in the past 40 years due to the large areal extent of the storm.  Farther to the south and west the precipitation fell as rain.  Enough rain fell to cause some minor flooding on the Chariton and Middle Rivers.  The Middle River crested about a foot over flood state in Indianola, while the Chariton River crested a little over 2 feet over flood stage in Chariton.

A strong upper level low pressure system moved from the Rockies on the 22nd, and across much of the Upper Midwest from the 23rd to the 25th. A large swath of heavy snow accompanied by sustained winds in the 15 to 20 mph range were noted across much of Central and South Central Minnesota. Some notable snow totals include: 17.5 inches at Hewitt (Todd County), 17.0 inches at New London (Kandiyohi County) and St. James (Watonwan County), 16.5 inches at 10 miles N of Mora (Kanabec County), 15.5 inches at Hutchinson (McLeod County), 14.0 inches at Albert Lea (Freeborn County), and 12.2 inches at Chanhassen (Carver County).

A powerful storm system moved through the upper midwest in late February, and brought heavy snow to much of northeast Minnesota with localized blizzard conditions along the north shore of Lake Superior. The snow began late on the 23rd in the Cass and Brainerd Lakes area, and ended on the evening of the 25th. Snowfall of 12 to 14 inches occured at the head of Lake Superior from Two Harbors to Cloquet, as well as across the Cass and Brainerd Lakes area, through southern Aitkin County and into western Pine County. Areas from the Iron Range to northern and eastern areas of the arrowhead received less than 2 inches. In addition to the heavy snow, blizzard conditions occured across the north shore during the early morning hours of the 25th, with winds gusting 40 to 50 mph. Many churches in Duluth cancelled Sunday morning services because of blowing and drifting snow.

Blizzard conditions were reported over eastern Colorado and parts of northwest Kansas and southwest Nebraska during the day.  The period of most intense snow lasted about 3-5 hours at any given location as winds gusted over 60 mph.  One peak gust was measured at 75 mph in Cheyenne Wells, CO.
Whiteout conditions reported with visibility to 100 yards.

Snow drifts up to 3 feet deep were reported. Prior to the closure of Interstate 70, the icy conditions and zero visibilities caused a 35-car pileup, just east of Denver near E-470. Rows: A storm system brought locally heavy rain, which fell on already saturated soil from previous snow and ice melt. This resulted in flooding in portions of central Missouri, February 24th through February 26th. It included the lower Grand, Chariton, Platte, and Blackwater Rivers, and Moniteau and Petite Saline Creeks.
The Petite Saline Creek near Boonville crested at 18.25 feet, or 2.25 feet above flood stage.

Rows: A powerful storm system moved through the upper midwest in late February, and brought heavy snow to much of northeast Minnesota with localized blizzard conditions along the north shore of Lake Superior. The snow began late on the 23rd in the Cass and Brainerd Lakes area, and ended on the evening of the 25th. Snowfall of 12 to 14 inches occured at the head of Lake Superior from Two Harbors to Cloquet, as well as across the Cass and Brainerd Lakes area, through southern Aitkin County and into western Pine County. Areas from the Iron Range to northern and eastern areas of the arrowhead received less than 2 inches. In addition to the heavy snow, blizzard conditions occured across the north shore during the early morning hours of the 25th, with winds gusting 40 to 50 mph. Many churches in Duluth cancelled Sunday morning services because of blowing and drifting snow.
A prolonged winter storm dumped 15 to 30 inches of new snow on the South Washington Cascades.

A 2 day Pacific storm dumped 15 to 30 inches of new snow on the South Washington Cascades. Near Mt St Helens Swift Creek reported 32 inches of new snow, June Lake 30 inches. Other locations reported 15 to 25 inches.|

Rows: A low pressure system moved across the area bringing very strong surface winds and light to moderate snow.  Blizzard conditions were reported over eastern Colorado and parts of northwest Kansas and southwest Nebraska during the day.  The period of most intense snow lasted about 3-5 hours at any given location as winds gusted over 60 mph.  One peak gust was measured at 75 mph in Cheyenne Wells, CO.
Visibility down to zero at times.

Rows: A strong upper level low pressure system moved from the Rockies on the 22nd, and across much of the Upper Midwest from the 23rd to the 25th. A large swath of heavy snow accompanied by sustained winds in the 15 to 20 mph range were noted across much of West Central Wisconsin. Some notable totals include 14 inches on the west side of Eau Claire (Eau Claire County), 3 S Island Lake (Chippewa County), and in Roberts (St. Croix County), 10.8 inches at Durand (Pepin County), 10 inches 2 S Clear Lake (Polk County), and 9 inches 2 S Rice Lake (Barron County).

Rows: A widespread and crippling ice/snow storm affected eastern Iowa, northwest and western Illinois, and extreme northeast Missouri on February 24, 2007. This massive ice storm was the worst to affect the region since January 22-23, 1965. Ice accumulations of around one inch were common, with some reports to near two inches! To make matters worse, east winds gusting over 50 mph, combined with the heavy ice accumulation, brought down numerous tree branches and power lines, along with several thousand power poles. There were even whole trees crashing down from the weight of the ice. Widespread power outages occurred, affecting over 180,000 people, which lasted more than a week in some of the rural areas. Many shelters were opened to accommodate those without power. The governor of Iowa declared much of the state a disaster area, and requested President Bush to declare much of eastern Iowa a federal disaster area. In the northern portions of the region in the colder air, snow was the problem. Accumulations of up to 7 inches occurred, with strong winds combining to create blizzard conditions. Considering the magnitude of the storm, remarkably no direct deaths were reported.
A spotter in Keosauqua reported 4 inch tree branches down around town. At Farmington, power was out with numerous large trees down blocking roads.

Rows: Widespread freezing rain developed on February 24th and produced ice accumulations of near or greater than a quarter inch. The freezing rain changed to snow by the night of the 24th, then moderate to heavy snow continued through the morning and into the early afternoon of February 25th. Snow accumulations ranged from 5 to 11 inches.

Widespread freezing rain produced ice accumulations near or above a quarter inch on February 24th. The icing made travel extremely difficult. The precipitation changed to snow late on the 24th, with snow accumulating 7 to 11 inches before ending by early afternoon on February 25th. The snow accumulations on top of the ice made travel impossible in places. The combination also caused tree branches and a few power lines to break, producing scattered power outages. Some weekend school activities were cancelled, as were several Sunday church services.

A strong low pressure system moved across the central Plains. The northern edge of this system brought heavy snow to south central South Dakota. The precipitation started as a mix of rain, freezing rain, and sleet before changing to snow. Six to 12 inches of snow fell across Tripp County and eastern portions of Mellette and Todd Counties, with the heaviest snow across northeastern Tripp County. Gusty northwest winds produced blowing and drifting snow and reduced visibilities to a quarter of a mile or less at times.

A strong area of low pressure tracking across the central plains brought widespread snowfall to parts of central and much of northeast South Dakota. The precipitation initially began as freezing rain and sleet late in the evening of the 23rd as it lifted across the area through the morning of the 24th. The freezing rain and sleet then changed over to snow during the morning hours of the 24th. Thundersnow also occurred at some locations across the area. Snowfall amounts of 6 to 15 inches had occurred as the storm ended. With the initial slippery roads from the freezing rain and then the heavy snow, travel conditions became very difficult. The State Emergency Management, Highway Patrol, and Department of Transportation issued a travel advisory for no travel for Interstate-90 and many highways in central South Dakota. There were numerous accidents along the interstate. Some snowfall amounts included, 9 inches at Bryant and Webster, 10 inches at Toronto, Roy Lake, and Garden City, 11 inches at Faulkton, 12 inches at Watertown, and 15 inches at Clear Lake.

Widespread rain and freezing rain developed on February 24th. Most of the freezing rain was northeast of a Sioux Center to Storm Lake line, and ice accumulations of a quarter inch or more resulted in the Spirit lake to Spencer area. The rain and freezing rain changed to snow on the night of February 24th, and snow continued through the morning of February 25th. Snow accumulations ranged from 4 to 11 inches, except for lesser amounts in the Ida Grove to Storm Lake area. Travel was very difficult, especially in the heavy icing area, and in the area of the heaviest snow around Sioux City. There were several accidents, and numerous vehicles slid into ditches.

Freezing rain developed on February 24th and produced over a quarter inch of ice accumulation. The freezing rain changed to snow that night, with snow continuing through the morning of February 25th. The snow accumulated 5 to 8 inches. Travel was extremely difficult. Several weekend school activities and church services were cancelled.

Some notable totals include 14 inches on the west side of Eau Claire (Eau Claire County), 3 S Island Lake (Chippewa County), and in Roberts (St. Croix County), 10.8 inches at Durand (Pepin County), 10 inches 2 S Clear Lake (Polk County), and 9 inches 2 S Rice Lake (Barron County).

A late season cold front brought high winds to the south Oregon coast on this date.  A High Wind Warning was issued at 24/0350 PST, effective from 24/0350 to 24/1600 PST.  The warning was cancelled at 24/1139 PST, at which time the event was verifying.

Details.Description: Measured at Gold Beach.

Rows: A widespread and crippling ice/snow storm affected eastern Iowa, northwest and western Illinois, and extreme northeast Missouri on February 24, 2007. This massive ice storm was the worst to affect the region since January 22-23, 1965. Ice accumulations of around one inch were common, with some reports to near two inches! To make matters worse, east winds gusting over 50 mph, combined with the heavy ice accumulation, brought down numerous tree branches and power lines, along with several thousand power poles. There were even whole trees crashing down from the weight of the ice. Widespread power outages occurred, affecting over 180,000 people, which lasted more than a week in some of the rural areas. Many shelters were opened to accommodate those without power. In the northern portions of the region in the colder air, snow was the problem. Accumulations of up to 7 inches occurred, with strong winds combining to create blizzard conditions. There was one direct death and one indirect serious injury due to the ice storm in northwest Illinois.

Rows: Strong northwest winds developed across the west central South Dakota plains as a intense storm system moved across the Central Plains. Winds were strongest in the Rapid City area and adjacent plains, where wind gusts around 60 mph were recorded.
